title: Review: Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask

The post Review: Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
South Africa’s James Sedgwick Distillery is no stranger to experimental cask finishing, and given Chenin Blanc is the country’s most widely-planted grape varietal, it was only a matter of time before someone paired these casks with a whisky to represent something uniquely South African.

Released as the seventh addition to the Three Ships Master’s Collection, this whisky is produced from column-distilled malt and aged in American oak casks of varying ages before resting in Chenin Blanc wine casks for two years.

Three Ships 6 Years Old Chenin Blanc Cask Review

The nose is bright, inviting, and strikes a beautiful balance between spirit and cask. Initially it
offers a typical bourbon cask signature, while the wine cask’s fingerprint takes a little longer
to settle. The balance of oak, malt sweetness, and vanilla, blended with the excitement of
lemon zest, peach, and grapefruit, makes for an enjoyable aromatic experience. There’s also
a perfumed note present on the nose which blends well between the fruit and oak aromas,
however, some may find it unpleasant.

On the palate, the Chenin Blanc cask finish is more evident. It hits with sweet honey and
vanilla upfront, followed by vibrant pineapple, pear, apple, and a bright citrus tang to cut
through the body and carries through to the finish. Ginger builds gradually, adding structure
rather than heat. The finish leaves behind orchard fruit, soft spice, drying oak, and a slight
minerality.

What is most impressive about this whisky is its balance. It’s easy for a wine cask to steal
some spotlight from the spirit. However, here the Chenin Blanc casks brighten the
whisky’s profile, enhancing freshness while maintaining the character of the spirit. This
finish feels purposeful rather than experimental, and this one is easily one of my favorite
wine cask finishes.

This expression reinforces Three Ships’ reputation as a leading brand of South African
whisky. This edition is distinctive without chasing novelty and offers incredible value for
money. It’s available for around $45 and should appeal to whisky enthusiasts looking for
something beyond sherry and Port finishes, or perhaps an everyday summer dram.

86 proof.

B+ / $45

title: Review: First West Explorer Bourbon
summary:

(Turns out these are also historically inspired by the…

The post Review: First West Explorer Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Once bottled as part of the 15 Stars empire, First West just spun itself out into its own brand (though “crafted by 15 Stars” still appears on the label in small print), complete with different branding and a weird-looking bottle that reminds me of a fish. (Turns out these are also historically inspired by the bottles of yore.)

While the corporate branding is its own — First West being a reference to how Kentucky was the first stop on the westward expansion into the frontier — the production process is really the same: Like 15 Stars, these are sourced Kentucky whiskeys, at least for the most part. The brand now contains four expressions, of which we received one: Explorer. With Explorer, its a four-grain blend of Kentucky straight bourbon at least 5 years old that is “blended with our own baby black corn bourbons for improved flavor.” It’s unclear what those black corn bourbons refer to here, or who produces it, but I suspect there’s little to be gained by speculating on that front, anyway.

Let’s taste it.

First West Explorer Bourbon Review

After a somewhat brash attack on the nose, Explorer manages to air itself out a bit and tame what feels like a bit of a beast. Unfortunately, what’s left behind is a little scattered — butterscotch and caramel corn, quite sweet, backed up by lumberyard and black pepper aromas, some earthy greenery ringing the edges.

The palate is a contrast: All corn, or nearly all corn, anyway. Here the caramel corn finds loads of fresh-popped popcorn folded in, first coming across as quite savory before the whiskey’s natural sweetness grows anew and evolves further into candied territory, evoking peanut brittle dipped in cinnamon syrup. The midpalate is otherwise indistinct, showing a bit of mint and some cherry Sucrets notes, before a somewhat short, slightly underdeveloped conclusion. Ultimately this winds up as one of those whiskeys that feels mostly harmless and otherwise indistinct, though nothing at which I’d turn my nose up at happy hour.

95 proof.

B / $50

The post Review: Rhum Barbancourt Haitian Proof appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
“Haitian proof'” for this white rum from Barbancourt is 110, a healthy abv for this product made from pressed cane juice and bottled without aging and filtering, which is similar for (similar) agricole-style rums.

Rhum Barbancourt Haitian Proof Review

While this is intended largely as a cocktail ingredient, the rum is surprisingly agreeable, even served solo and at full strength. The nose has a gentle hogo note but is otherwise dominated by overripe pineapple and coconut cream, becoming increasingly prominent as it sits in glass. Air time helps notes of green banana and a lightly grassy quality — much less present than in agricole, thanks to the high proof — come into focus.

The palate offers similar qualities, banana a bit more clearly evident, with a lemongrass note following behind. The body is a bit more obviously cane-based than the nose suggests, with overt sweetness and a couple of extra upticks of green grass opening the door to some more clearly pastoral qualities. The finish sees lingering sugar, with cinnamon a distant echo. The fade-out is clean but enduringly sweet, with hints of butterscotch.

This is solid stuff and, given the abv, quite versatile, too. For the price (usually under $20), it’s one of the best white rums you’re likely to find, in any style of production.

110 proof.

A- / $18 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: A Visit to the Wineries of Bordeaux, 2026
summary:
Nowhere in the world is more synonymous with fine wine than Bordeaux, France, and this year I was finally fortunate enough to make a pilgrimage here and visit some of the most storied appellations and chateaux that exist. Bordeaux is both a region and a city, and the urban hub is larger and more vibrant…

The post A Visit to the Wineries of Bordeaux, 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Nowhere in the world is more synonymous with fine wine than Bordeaux, France, and this year I was finally fortunate enough to make a pilgrimage here and visit some of the most storied appellations and chateaux that exist.

Bordeaux is both a region and a city, and the urban hub is larger and more vibrant than you’d think, a full-fledged metro that is reminiscent of Paris writ small. It’s filled with cafes and restaurants and tourists who arrive by river cruise – and on one night during our visit, a music festival headlined by The Cure.

Getting out of town and to wineries means hiring a driver (or taking a tour) or, as we did, renting a car. It’s easy enough to navigate the area, but you’ll soon see that Bordeaux is a huge, and visiting the entirety of region will probably require a week or more. In the end, I visited the Medoc and the St. Emilion areas to get a better sense of classic Left Bank and Right Bank terroir and winemaking, sad to miss out on the southern portions of the Left Bank, particularly Sauternes.

Wine tourism still feels like a bit of a novel idea here. I contacted over a dozen wineries before my trip, months in advance, attempting to set up media visits. A large number never responded to my inquiries. Even Bordeaux’s trade group referred me to its website to research who might be open for a visit. Eventually I made appointments with five chateaux (or seven depending on how you count) over the two days of touring. For the record, none offered any special comps for press; I paid for tours and/or tastings at every stop, with prices ranging from 9 to 60 euros per person. (As one fellow traveler remarked to me during a tasting: “In Bordeaux you won’t get anything for free. Not so much as a breadstick.”)

Every winery we visited proclaimed that thanks to the scorching heat of 2026 this year was its earliest harvest in history. There’s no telling how that will pan out when the wine hits the bottle, but it’s certainly yet another thing for winemakers to have to worry about.

Here’s a look at each winery we visited, along with thoughts on the experience – and the wines.

Left Bank

Chateau Leoville Barton and Langoa Barton, St. Julien

The Barton family operates these two wineries across the street from one another, with tastings held jointly. A third winery, Chateau Mauvesin Barton, which is situated just north of Bordeaux in Moulis-en-Medoc, is also featured. The wineries date back to the 1820s, with both creating wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Cabernet Franc. As is common on the west/left side of the Garonne River, Cabernet dominates all blends.

Fully remodeled in 2020-21, the Barton operation has jumped dramatically in sophistication, and our guide kindly walked us through the grounds, winemaking, and cellars (surprisingly compact and often empty-feeling, a commonality across Bordeaux) before offering six wines to taste, including vertical looks at Langoa (2007 vs. 2016) and Leoville (2005 vs. 2014). I was a fan of both Langoa wines, bright with chocolate and cherry, with the younger Langoa showing a more acidic edge, as well as the 2005 Leoville, laced with mint and herbs. The 2014 Leoville fell quite flat, however, its fruit already fading badly.

33250 Saint-Julien-Beychevelle, France

Chateau Phelan Segur, St. Estephe

We were otherwise alone during our visit to this blue chip winery, a few miles south of St. Julien, and here got our first chance to step into the actual vineyards. While St. Estephe is described as gravelly, I wasn’t prepared for what were actually huge stones on the ground, smooth rocks that look like something you’d see in a decorative garden. These stones – all natural – warm the soil and the vines underneath. Cabernet appears to love the heat.

Phelan Segur adds Petit Verdot to its trio of grapes, but again Cabernet Sauvignon is the focus, usually comprising 55-65% of a blend. In the vineyard, 121 plots of grapes are designated, and each is vinified separately before blending after maturation.

To taste, the winery offered three vintages of Phelan Segur – 2023, 2018, and 2017 – plus a sample of 2016 Frank Phelan, its second label. Of the three, I slightly preferred the 2018 to 2017, the wine rich with black fruit and a massive kick of licorice on the palate before leading into a hearty, chocolatey finish. The 2017 is brighter and a little sweeter, maintaining a familiar resemblance to the young 2023. As for Frank Phelan, this more affordable wine – becoming increasingly common in Bordeaux – is a much different experience, offering fruit and vanilla notes that taste decidedly New World.

Rue des Écoles, 33180 Saint-Estèphe, France

Right Bank

In contrast to the many villages of the Left Bank, the fairly large St. Emilion dominates the Right Bank, where Merlot is king (and mandated to comprise at least half of each blend). Unlike the virtually flat Left Bank, the Right Bank is steeply hilly and dominated by the village of St. Emilion, a UNESCO site that feels ripped out of the Middle Ages.

Chateau La Croizille and Chateau Tour Baladoz, St. Emilion

If you do any amount of research into “best wineries to visit in Bordeaux,” Chateau La Croizille always comes up. Credit strong SEO skills for that. I’d never heard of either of these wineries previously, but I didn’t sweat much about that since there are some 800 wine producers in the region. Only a fraction of those have a presence in the U.S.

The operation does offer an interesting promise: La Croizille is very modern, having been redeveloped in 2012. Baladoz is more traditional in its production processes. They have the same ownership and are right next to one another, so you get to see two sides of Bordeaux winemaking in one trip.

Baladoz is particularly interesting since it uses all six approved Bordeaux grapes in its wines – though I found its 2009 sample to come across as badly oxidized, perhaps because it was left over from the previous day or two. A 2022 bottle was much fresher and more exciting. Otherwise I preferred the 2010 La Croizille sample, which is made of just 55% Merlot, 45% Cabernet Sauvignon. Softer and more refined, it’s perhaps small evidence that modern winemaking may help make better wine.

We opted for a “winemaker’s picnic” at this stop, but that turned out to be a pair of small cheese and charcuterie baskets intended to be eaten at the winery, sans winemaker. That was fine, as the views here are fantastic.

810 route du Tertre anciennement lieu-dit “Baladoz, 33330 Saint-Laurent-des-Combes, France

Chateau Cantenac, St. Emilion

We didn’t have time for a tour at tiny Cantenac, but we got the full story and some tastings from A.J., the wife of one of the family members who run this homey operation. (The winery is run by its matriarch, and its three sons all married interns who passed through its doors.)

The wines here are hearty despite being heavy on the Merlot (80% is common), the 2022 Grand Cru quite oak-forward with well-developed tannins and notes of aged cheese. A softer experience awaits in the Selection Madame expression, crafted to the tastes of the owner. This can be 95 to 100% Merlot, the 2021 showing brighter fruit and pushy florals, with some herbs and pepper adding spice to the mix.

Of special note, the tasting here was just 9 euros per person, by far the cheapest of the trip.

719 Route de Castillon, 33330 Saint-Émilion, France

Chateau Troplong Mondot, St. Emilion

We had a private tour of the grounds and winery at this highly regarded winery, including a lengthy visit through the vineyard to taste Merlot off the vine and ogle the extremely rocky soil – covered with stones as big as my fist. The view is another big reason to come here: Troplong Mondot is situated on the highest point in St. Emilion, and you can see the town of St. Emilion below from up on high, a unique perspective.

After a tour of its modernized winery (which works with 85% Merlot, 12% Cabernet Sauvignon, and 3% Cabernet Franc as its blending palette), we tucked into four wines, including a 2021 Mondot (second label) and three vintages of the Grand Cru – 2020, 2018, and 2015.

Of all the tastings on this trip, this was the most complex and instructive at showcasing how widely vintages can vary in Bordeaux. 2015 and 2020 were both deep, intense, and well-structured wines that were nods to the rule that every fifth year is a knockout vintage in the region. I had trouble picking a favorite between the two, which showed off lively cherry notes and silky tannins – though the 2015 ultimately leans on some heavier complexity. The 2018 in contrast came across as a bit barnyardy, with a hefty turned earth quality – probably closer to the experience that many people think of when Bordeaux comes to mind.

Bonus points to Troplong for its elegant, personal tasting experience. While on the pricy side, it’s a visit that’s definitely worth it.

33330 Saint-Laurent-des-Combes, France

The post A Visit to the Wineries of Bordeaux, 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.

title: Review: Boplaas 1880 Single Grain Whisky 6 Years Old Tawny Port Cask Finish
summary:
Based in the town of Calitzdorp in the Western Cape of South Africa, the Boplaas Family Vineyards is a sixth-generation estate with distilling history stretching as far back as 1880. They are best known for producing Port-style wines and award-winning pot still brandies, but have recently made waves in the South African whisky scene, and…

The post Review: Boplaas 1880 Single Grain Whisky 6 Years Old Tawny Port Cask Finish appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Based in the town of Calitzdorp in the Western Cape of South Africa, the Boplaas Family Vineyards is a sixth-generation estate with distilling history stretching as far back as 1880. They are best known for producing Port-style wines and award-winning pot still brandies, but have recently made waves in the South African whisky scene, and have collected a couple of international awards across their range.

This 6 year old single grain is produced from local yellow maize and matured in a combination of ex-bourbon and tawny Port casks. Bottled at 43% abv and sitting within the medium-bodied, easy-drinking camp, this expression is one of six in the 1880 range of grain and malt whiskies, each matured in different casks and at varying ages. The area’s hot/dry summers, cold winters, and relatively low humidity encourage an almost rapid style of maturation. The tradeoff is a generous angels’ share, but a surprisingly flavorful spirit bottled at a comparatively young age.

Boplaas 1880 Single Grain Whisky 6 Years Old Tawny Port Cask Finish Review

The first impression is inviting. The nose opens with fruit cake, dried figs, apricot, and a gentle mix of winter spices. There is a great balance of oak to spirit balance on the nose, which I feel is important: Port-finished whiskies can often feel a little cask-heavy. Here, the tawny influence is beautifully integrated. The ex-bourbon maturation provides a classic vanilla and oak foundation, while the port finish adds dried fruit and a rounded sweetness without completely overwhelming the grain spirit.

On the palate, this whisky is well-rounded and pleasantly chewy. Bright orchard fruit, floral notes, and spices lead the way. The spirit is a little aggressive, but certainly isn’t thin – I feel the abv of 43% was a wise choice here. The finish is medium in length with lingering oak spice, toffee warmth, and gentle sweetness. It’s not an incredibly complex whisky, but it’s satisfying and coherent. There’s enough happening here to make it interesting, and again, the lower abv keeps it approachable and perfect for casual sipping.

Overall, this is a great whisky to display the Boplaas house style, appealing to drinkers who enjoy bourbon, Irish whiskey, or Scotch styles. This bottling is a useful reminder than single grain whisky isn’t always bland – the spirit itself is relatively quiet, but the maturation has given it plenty personality.

Available at an incredibly accessible price, the Boplaas 1880 Single Grain Whisky 6 Years Old Tawny Port Cask Finish makes a strong case as an everyday sipping whisky rather, and also works great for gifting. This bottle will stay on my shelf for guests who want something easy-drinking, or looking to explore the growing South African whisky category.

This is an approachable South African single grain with a well-integrated tawny cask influence. Fruity, lightly spiced, and easy to enjoy. This whisky offers good value and an exciting introduction to Boplaas’ range. A solid sipper that punches above its price point.

86 proof.

B+ / $40

title: The 19 Best Whiskeys We Tasted at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival 2026
summary:
The Kentucky Bourbon Festival celebrated its 35th year last weekend and once again took over the small town, bourbon epicenter of Bardstown. While the recent sales sheets may say otherwise, bourbon still has a massive and dedicated following that turned out in a big way, a sold-out 6,000 strong, to wait in the heat and…

The post The 19 Best Whiskeys We Tasted at the Kentucky Bourbon Festival 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The Kentucky Bourbon Festival celebrated its 35th year last weekend and once again took over the small town, bourbon epicenter of Bardstown. While the recent sales sheets may say otherwise, bourbon still has a massive and dedicated following that turned out in a big way, a sold-out 6,000 strong, to wait in the heat and occasional rain for a chance to taste, and just maybe purchase, their favorite Kentucky whiskeys.

Perhaps the biggest thing that stood out about this year’s festival was the embarrassment of riches available to whiskey fans from both legacy distillers and a broad lineup of craft and non-distilling producers, many of whom were sampling some of the most talked about bottles of the weekend. Compared to my last visit in 2023, the excitement for smaller Kentucky distillers was palpable with the Craft Distillers’ Row area of the festival boasting some of the biggest crowds of the weekend.

As usual, there was more whiskey on hand for even the most dedicated fan to catalogue, but I did my level best in between much-needed water breaks, a few engaging industry talks on the main stage, the occasional premium event (a great way to grab some AC), and trying to get a picture with Jim Gaffigan (struck out) who was at the festival promoting his Fathertime bourbon brand (and maybe also Hot Pockets). Chris was able to narrow it to 17 best last year, but I didn’t have that kind of self restraint. At least I kept it under 20!

Booker’s The Reserves 2026

The latest Booker’s The Reserves release was one of Beam’s rarer offerings during the festival, and while it didn’t quite sing like the Knob Creek Single Barrel pick selected for the festival, it was still one of the more memorable pours of the night. Inspired by a Booker Noe holiday wassail, this 6-year rye was aged in French apple brandy casks and infused with cinnamon sticks, delivering loads of warm baking spice and green Jolly Rancher notes for days. We haven’t seen a rye whiskey with a Booker’s label on it since the 13-year “Big Time Batch” a decade ago. This wasn’t that. But it was a lot of fun. $130

Kentucky Boy Straight Bourbon Whiskey

The longest lines every day of the festival were to taste, and more importantly purchase, this bottle. That’s understandable since limited editions from Brown-Forman are rarely both interesting and affordable. Kentucky Boy honors the 50-year career of Kentucky legend and master distiller emeritus Chris Morris. It’s an unspecified blend of Woodford Double Oak, Old Forester Birthday Bourbon, and King of Kentucky, and if you think that sounds like a bold and oak-forward bourbon, you’d be right. Chocolate, ginger, and barrel char dominated this decidedly rustic yet quite enjoyable, commemorative pour. $100

Dark Arts Mizunara 19 Year Old

Dark Arts was once again a darling of the festival with lines almost as long as the Brown-Forman tent. And in many cases fans were shelling out considerably more money for their bottles, like this luxe rendition of their acclaimed Mizunara Bourbon that was aged a whopping 19 years and finished in Mizunara casks before bottling at cast strength. Mizunara and old bourbon shouldn’t work this well together, but this was an impressively balanced and full-flavored bourbon, silky on the palate with beautiful notes of brown butter and five spice. $400

Wilderness Trail Wheated Bourbon 10 Years Old

This 10-year-old, wheated bourbon blend was a highlight of the festival, bottled to celebrate the induction of Wilderness Trail co-founders Shane Baker and Pat Heist into the Kentucky Bourbon Hall of Fame. Before Wilderness Trail scaled up production of their impressive bourbons and ryes, they fine-tuned their unique sweet-mash process on a small pot still. This wheated bourbon is some of the earliest and best whiskey to come off that still, delivering a bold yet balanced mix of classic bourbon flavors from rich brown sugar to caramel apple and pie spice. $190

Silk Velvet Barrel Proof Single Barrel Whiskey

Maybe the most talked about craft distiller at the festival this year, Silk Velvet offered a full lineup of great pours including a new, standout rye whiskey. But this seven-year-old, single barrel bourbon stole the opening night crown (as evidenced by the near sellout before the festival had even officially started). Made from a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley by eighth generation distiller Jacob Call (of early Green River fame), it was the biggest, boldest yet approachable bourbon of the festival for me. $100

MGP Chapter One: Out of the Shadows 10 Years Old

For decades, MGP has been the source for hundreds of whiskey brands, and now the storied distillery is finally taking its rightful place on the bourbon shelf with this new release, somewhat dramatically titled Chapter One: Out of the Shadows. It’s a 10-year-old blend of the distillery’s signature, high-rye mashbill bourbon bottled at a generous proof that showcases a healthy amount of baking spice, brown sugar, and black cherry, everything fans have come to love about the former Seagrams outpost. Now they can finally get it straight from the source. $70

K.Luke Batch 16 Bourbon

This was my first taste of K.Luke, and I have to say I was impressed. A passion project for founder Jonathan Maisono (who was doing all the pouring), the brand is the result of a single barrel obsession that led him to sample thousands of whiskeys and hone his blending skills. All that tasting clearly trained him well because this bourbon was impressively approachable without sacrificing an ounce of flavor. A blend of whiskey sourced from Kentucky and Indiana distilleries, aged at least 8 years, and bottled at just shy of 115 proof, it ticked all the classic bourbon boxes. $100

Very Olde St. Nick Superfreak Freakazoid

Preservation Distillery was one of the busiest tents at the festival and for good reason. They were pouring a long list of pricey unicorns including several humorously named expressions of their popular Very Olde St. Nick label. While the 19-year-old Notorious “The Shiz” seemed to be a favorite among those lucky enough to sample from the $1100 bottle, I personally preferred the more reasonably priced (comparatively) Superfreak Freakazoid. Like last year’s Superfreak, this was a blend of bourbons meant to showcase balance across a broad age range (11-18 years). And it succeeded, delivering layers of fruit and brighter sweetness while still showcasing a lot of maturity with a soothing, well-aged foundation of sandalwood and gingery spice. $350

New Riff Silver Grove

New Riff has been celebrating their double-digit age statement bourbons and ryes for a bit now, which is why this 6-year-old, barrel proof limited edition caught my eye. Released exclusively at the distillery in Newport, this young-ish bourbon (6 years old) is made with 30% malted rye and offered flavors you don’t usually get from New Riff including lots of sweet baked apple and candy apple notes.

Old Louisville Double Oak Rye

Old Louisville Whiskey Company had been on my radar for a few years now, but this was my first chance to sample their wares. They are a non-distilling producer that focuses on well-aged whiskeys, mostly sourced from MGP. I thought I liked several of their bourbons more than this double oaked rye, especially their 12-year-old festival release, but after sitting with it for a bit it really came to life. Made from 51% rye and 49% malted barley, it started out with that classic Kentucky-style rye profile – minted syrup and clove – but took on an impressive, earthy depth with a little time in the glass. $NA

WhistlePig 10 Year Bourbon Rye Cask Finish

WhistlePig, long known for their rye, seems equally serious now about bourbon. They made the move to sourced Kentucky stock last year and earlier this year opened an impressive tasting room dubbed The Vault in a former bank building in Louisville’s NULU neighborhood. Plenty of worthy WhistlePig rye was on offer over the weekend, but their newest bourbon, which won’t roll out until next year, was a standout. This 10-year ups the proof from previous WhistlePig bourbons while adding warm top notes of clove and ginger with a finishing in their rye casks. $NA

Angel’s Envy Cellar Collection 2026

Under master distiller Owen Martin, Angel’s Envy has continued to push the boundaries of cask finishing. Some of these experimental whiskeys have been better than others, but the upcoming 2026 Cellar Collection, a rye finished in peach brandy and toasted oak barrels, is going to have a lot fans. It was hiding behind a few tables at the festival, and I managed to sneak a taste. Peach is one of my favorite flavors, and this has it in spades with peach rings candy on the nose and a palate that adds depth across the sip from fresh peaches and cream to warm peach cobbler. $NA

Michter’s Toasted Barrel Finish Rye

The Michter’s line was also one of the longer over the festival weekend with fans clamoring for the chance to taste and buy the 10-year bourbon and rye along with the latest Toasted Barrel Finish Rye release, a whiskey we haven’t seen since 2023. While a lot of distillers struggle to move their rye offerings, Michter’s can’t seem to make enough of it, and it’s easy to see why with this release; a big, toasty rye whiskey with layers of chocolate and baking spice accented by Andes mints and brûléed sugar. $120

Pursuit United Sakura Bloom Bourbon

The buzz over at the Pursuit Spirits tent was the cutely named “Found Footage,” a collaboration blend of their United Double Oak Rye with Shortbarrel’s maple-finished Sapsquatch. That whiskey was fun but not nearly as unique as this bourbon which aged in Japanese sakura wood and delivered a wholly unique floral element. Bottled at cask strength, it delivered notes of cherry blossom, peaches and cream, and bright, airy red fruits, all wrapped in brown sugar and baking spice for one of the best bottled desserts of the festival. $90

Barrell Hazmat Decade 2 20 Years Old

The Barrell booth was awash in bottles both new and old, including the latest red label 12-year finished in Cognac casks and the 15-year Gray Label Seagrass from years ago. A pair of Decades Releases caught the attention of ageist and hazmat whiskey drinkers, myself included in that particular moment, and I didn’t regret sampling this 20-year blend of Canadian whiskeys finished in Spanish brandy and Hungarian oak casks. It takes a special Canadian whiskey to drink well over 140 proof, and this was it: complex with syrupy fruits and dark caramel and impossibly approachable at full volume. $200

Bluegrass Distillers Blue Corn Single Barrel

Last year, Chris enjoyed the Elkwood Reserve 17 Year from Bluegrass Distillers, and this year’s 19 Year single barrel of Barton juice was another stunner, if a bit pricey. For all of $75, this Blue Corn Single Barrel was probably one of the better values at the festival. Most blue corn whiskeys tend to have a pronounced grain profile that doesn’t always work, but this expression was impressively balanced. It showed as much fruit and baking spice as it did grain character with a generous and memorable corn pudding note. $75

Four Roses Small Batch Limited Edition 2026

Four Roses was sampling several standout single barrel picks along with the latest Experimental Series release, a honey barrel finish so new it was poured out of an unlabeled, handle-sized lab bottle. But the 2026 Small Batch Limited Edition was in short supply. If you were quick to the opening night lines or managed to find master distiller Brent Elliott throughout the weekend, you could luck into a sample. That pour featured some of the oldest Four Roses stock yet, a 23-year OESK that made up 10% of the blend and added a notable heft and depth to a whiskey that’s often more fruit-forward and high toned. Great stuff, once again. $250

Bardstown Bourbon Co. Discovery 2026

Bardstown Bourbon Co. was pouring most of its impressive portfolio, including the much-discussed Lochs of Jura finished in single malt casks. That bourbon was almost too nuanced to really dig into during a hot day of festival tasting, but the newest Discovery release did the trick, showing loads of bold rye spice with rich undertones of ginger snap cookies from the Garryana oak aging. $140

Calumet Farm 12 Years Old

Whiskey House was hard to miss with its two-story chalet front and center at the festival’s main gate. There were a multitude of standout options from the distillery’s many contract brands, including two Phifer Pavitt Cab-finished bourbons and the return of the delicious Calumet Farm 18 Years Old. This 12-year, small batch Calumet was a real surprise, however; a rare, noteworthy bourbon that delivered impressive flavor without any special finishing, crazy proof, or extra age. And at a reasonable price, to boot. $100

The post Review: Wilfa Performance Coffee Maker and Uniform Grinder appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Do you like coffee? The folks at Wilfa sure do, but even more than that the seem to enjoy eye-catching design. Almost Rube Goldbergian in its construction, the Wilfa Performance Coffee Maker looks like what futurists in the 1970s probably imagined a coffee maker would look like in the 2020s. And hey, maybe they were right!

The unit is surprisingly simple: Water in the carafe on the right. Grounds (weighed to the appropriate number of grams, naturally) and filter in the basket on the left. There’s only a single power button, no timer, to get it going. To set the amount of coffee you want, you twist an analog dial on the bottom of the filter basket.

Coffee comes out expeditiously, but as expected I found the results varied dramatically based on the coffee I used. Lardera, the North American partner for Wilfa, provided samples of 4 of its 11 single-origin coffees to use with the Wilfa system. Far and away my favorite was the Bourbon Washed offering from Peru; it’s not made with whiskey, but it had a slight mocha character, modest nuttiness, and a more nuanced flavor profile despite an overall bolder profile. I also enjoyed the Catuai Honey expression, grown in Costa Rica, which was quite fruity and a bit sweet, a much different experience than the Bourbon Washed. All coffees run about $2 for a 2-oz bag of whole bean coffee (good for about 4 or 5 cups).

Of course, you’ll need to grind those beans before you drink them, and Wilfa has you covered there, too, with a Uniform Grinder that costs more ($299) than the coffee maker ($249). This massive device, 15 inches tall and 7 pounds in weight, has 41 grinding level options, all dialed in by twisting the top of the device. Just dump in your beans and press the lonely start button. Grounds are deposited into a canister below. It’s quite effective, but the amount of counter space it takes up, like the Coffee Maker, is beyond excessive.

At $548 for the combination of coffee maker and grinder, this is a set of gear designed with absolute coffee nerds squarely in mind. While my tests over the course of a week with the system didn’t result in visibly more delicious coffee than I can get from a standard drip machine, its status as a conversation piece arguably filled in some of that gap.

Wilfa Performance Coffee Maker: B / $249 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]
Wilfa Uniform Grinder: B / $299

summary:

The post Review: Four Roses Limited Edition Small Batch Bourbon 2026 Edition appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
September is here, and while it has not brought with it anything in the way of cool weather, it has come along with the latest expression of Four Roses Limited Edition Small Batch Bourbon, the distillery’s most prized annual release and one which we have covered since its inauguration.

This 19th edition of the bourbon features some of the oldest stock ever to appear in the series, with the barrel strength release composed of four batches selected by master distiller Brent Elliott. Here’s the makeup:

• 14-year-old OBSK (31%)
• 14-year-old OESK (39%)
• 15-year-old OESV (20%)
• 23-year-old OESK (10%)

On paper, that’s a powerful lineup that makes it feel like Elliott may be swinging for the fences with this one. I’m all for it. Let’s see whether it connects.

Four Roses Limited Edition Small Batch Bourbon 2026 Edition Review

While last year’s release leaned on V yeast, this year we see a whiskey that is 80% K — designed to create a final product that is pushier on spice and less fruity. I’d say that was a success, the nose here overwhelming with the contents of the baking cabinet, particularly cinnamon and ground ginger. Close behind however is plenty of oak. That 23 year old stock may be limited to a mere 10% of the blend, but it’s quite dominant on the nose, giving the whiskey powerfully tannic aromas of dark chocolate and a peppery edge. Four Roses often leans on a reputation of softness, but this lands far from it.

At full proof the palate can come across as a bit hot, though I think that’s largely driven by the ultra-old stock in the mix, creating a gritty quality that makes the experience feel racier than it may actually be. While that peppery, herbal heat is present, ample notes of butterscotch and vanilla mix immediately to sweeten the pot, at first a bit bluntly, then in a more cohesive manner. Time in glass helps this whiskey immensely, coaxing out a dried floral character along with a more pastry-like baking spice that tastes modestly of Christmas cake. Wood is omnipresent, but the longer you sit with it, the more it fades into the background.

Bottom line: Want something more powerful than expected — maybe too powerful? — from your Four Roses special edition investment? Look no further.

109.2 proof. 16,800 bottles produced. Available starting October 10, 2026.

A- / $249 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

summary:

The first (and currently only) release comes from Wick in the Highlands and is limited to just 120 bottles. The distillery is undisclosed, although there’s not much…

The post Review: Old Towns of Scotland #01 – Wick appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Old Towns of Scotland is a new series of small-batch releases from South African retailer WhiskyBrother, each intended to showcase the character of a particular Scottish whisky-producing region.

The first (and currently only) release comes from Wick in the Highlands and is limited to just 120 bottles. The distillery is undisclosed, although there’s not much mystery for anyone familiar with Wick’s whisky history. This is a small-batch vatting of whiskies aged between 10 and 14 years, matured in ex-bourbon and ex-sherry casks and bottled at a punchy 50.5% abv (101 proof).

Old Towns of Scotland #01 – Wick Review

Some whiskies give you a pretty good idea of what’s coming before you even pull the cork, and this is one of them. The label’s busy Wick harbor, a nod to the town’s long history as a port for herring fishing, sets the tone nicely: coastal, rustic, and maritime. And, sure enough, that character comes through in the glass.

The nose is malt-forward and inviting, with biscuit, polished oak and toffee, backed by a touch of lemon zest. There’s also a distinct briny, sea-salt note lurking underneath, enough to bring classic Campbeltown malts to mind. As it sits in the glass, the whisky becomes increasingly expressive, with a little waxy character and a faint hint of dried fruit adding some extra depth. It’s a substantial nose without being particularly heavy.

On the palate, toffee apple leads the way, wrapped in a creamy, surprisingly rich texture. Darker fruit emerges with time, joined by plenty of vanilla and a gentle hit of spice. There’s a nice balance between the sweeter, dessert-like notes and the more savory maritime character, with the higher abv giving everything a little extra weight. It’s certainly not shy, but the alcohol is reasonably well integrated and doesn’t overwhelm the underlying malt character.

The whisky also benefits from a little time in the glass. What initially presents as a fairly straightforward combination of sweetness and coastal character develops into something more layered, particularly as the darker fruit and oak become more pronounced. A few drops of water soften the edges and bring out more of the vanilla and citrus, although I preferred the fuller texture and intensity at full strength.

The finish brings burnt sugar and oak, followed by a pleasant dryness that lingers nicely. There’s a touch of spice here too, along with that persistent salty character, giving the finish more staying power than you might expect from a relatively young whisky.

This is a very good maritime malt that avoids the obvious trap of turning the coastal character into a one-note exercise in salt and oil. There’s plenty of fruit, sweetness, and oak here to keep things interesting, too. At 50.5% alcohol, it has enough muscle to stand up to a splash of water, although I’d happily drink it neat.

For a first release, Old Towns of Scotland #01 makes a pretty compelling case for the series. The undisclosed provenance is fun, but ultimately beside the point: What matters is that there’s an enjoyable, characterful whisky in the bottle. With only 120 bottles available, this is one worth seeking out while you can.

101 proof.

A / $80

This is a particularly fun whiskey because it can sometimes deliver more classic rye character, brighter and more herbal (like in 2024 and 2025), and sometimes it skews darker, more…

The post Review: Michter’s Single Barrel Straight Rye 10 Years Old 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Michter’s 10-year-old, single barrel rye has been a sought-after annual release for more than a decade now, and earlier this summer it returned once again. This is a particularly fun whiskey because it can sometimes deliver more classic rye character, brighter and more herbal (like in 2024 and 2025), and sometimes it skews darker, more of a bourbon drinker’s rye, as in 2023. Single barrel offerings are always going to vary slightly from barrel to barrel and year to year, even from a distillery known for its consistency like Michter’s. One thing never changes though. It’s always an easy drinking, well-balanced whiskey that manages to hit the sweet spot for well-aged rye. Let’s see what the 2026 release has in store.

Michter’s Single Barrel Straight Rye 10 Years Old 2026 Review

The nose is a bit of a contrast to previous years. It’s less high tone with a more restrained herbal element; more damp grass and soft wintergreen, less bright mint and fresh herbs. The oak is perhaps masking some of that greenery as there are lots of exotic wood notes in the mix: cedar and sandalwood with plenty of warm baking spice to back it up and a nice lacing of cocoa powder and a citrusy pop of Seville orange peel. There is a notable energy here that should be familiar to fans of older ryes, but it’s framed more by notes of butterscotch, toffee, and dark brown sugar which add a generous depth to the bouquet.

The palate is also a bit less rye-forward than in previous iterations with early notes of Demerara syrup, toffee, clove, and subtle blackberry jam. A bit of woody, cinnamon stick adds some grip on an otherwise lush and rich midpalate accented by dark notes of treacle, baking chocolate, and orange oil. A flash of rye spice arrives on the finish with fading notes of butter mints, eucalyptus, and a cool kiss of wintergreen, all underpinned by a decadent, sticky vanilla bean note that lingers long after the warmth has subsided. It’s another impressive, well-aged rye from Michter’s that should be universally appreciated by bourbon and rye lovers alike.

92.8 proof.

A- / $210 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]
